title: Learning and labor (Avot 2:2)
hookLine: study joined with work is good; together they keep wrongdoing away
carry: two hands, each keeping the other steady

cards: There are two ways to get stuck. One person reads every book about changing their life and never changes a thing: all ideas, floating.
Another works twelve-hour days, head down, and hasn't had a new thought in years: all motion, no meaning. Plenty of people lean one way or the other, depending on the season.
Today's sage is the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, the man who gathered the Mishnah. His saying: learning alone isn't enough.

teach.b: He's Rabban Gamaliel, and he opens with praise: beautiful is the study of Torah together with derekh eretz, because the effort of both keeps sin out of mind. Derekh eretz literally means the way of the land.
Elsewhere it means good manners; here it means earning a living, a trade, the ordinary work of the world.

teach.h: TWO KINDS OF EFFORT KEEP SIN AWAY.
teach.b: Why would the two together keep wrongdoing away? One reading is simple: a mind busy with learning and hands busy with work don't leave much room for trouble. But there's more.
Learning keeps work honest, because you bring what you've learned to the market and the workshop. Work keeps learning honest, because you have to live the ideas with real people and real money.
Then the warning side: Torah study without work, Gamaliel says, ends in nothing and brings sin along with it.
That's a strong line, and Jews have discussed the balance ever since.
The Talmud records two sages who disagreed: one said plow and plant in season, and study too; the other worried that if people are always plowing, when will the Torah get learned?
Today, some Jews combine a job with regular study, and some communities support people who study full-time as a sacred calling. Each side reads this saying closely.
What they share is Gamaliel's picture: learning and labor aren't enemies. They're two hands, and each keeps the other steady.

how: Some Jews combine a profession with regular Torah study, often a set time each day or week, while some communities support full-time study as a calling; both look to sayings like Avot 2:2.

games.q: you're a young student who loves learning. your trade takes hours every day. what does Rabban Gamaliel advise?
o: quit the trade and only study.
keep both, learning and labor together.
work now, and study when you retire.
games.why: beautiful is Torah study with derekh eretz, he says: the effort of both keeps sin out of mind.

practice: Think of something you've learned recently, anywhere, even from one of these sayings; small ones count. Then think of the work waiting for you today, paid or unpaid: a meeting, a shift, a conversation with a customer or a child.
Picture the idea showing up right there, the two meeting.
